questions.stem: An 84 year old widower who lives alone is seen by his GP after two falls. He feels tired all the time and a leg wound from 6 weeks ago has not healed. His trousers are loose and he has had three chest infections this winter. His BMI is 17.6 kg/m². His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. TSH is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An elderly man living alone with low BMI, weight loss, fatigue, falls, poor wound healing and frequent infections is malnourished.

steps.x: Weight loss, **falls**, **poor wound healing**, **frequent infections**, low BMI in an at-risk group.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Malnutrition.

elim: No breathlessness or raised JVP, and it does not explain the weight loss.
TSH is normal, and hypothyroidism causes weight gain.
Gives shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, not weight loss and poor healing.
Explains falls only, not the weight loss, infections and poor healing.

steps.x: **C. Malnutrition.** Falls + poor healing + infections + low BMI in an older person living alone = malnutrition.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has lost 14 kg over 4 months. She eats a few mouthfuls at each meal and gets breathless climbing one flight of stairs, which she managed easily before. Her BMI is 16.8 kg/m². Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Coarse facial features with large hands
questions.e: Cancer is a common cause of malnutrition; cachexia with muscle wasting and reduced exercise tolerance are the classic signs.

steps.x: Cancer + major weight loss + poor intake = **cachexia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Muscle wasting.

elim: Cushing's syndrome, the opposite of cachexia.
Not a feature of malnutrition.
Acromegaly.
Suggests lymphoma, not cachexia.

steps.x: **E. Temporal and limb muscle wasting.** Signs of malnutrition: cachexia, muscle wasting, hair thinning, pressure sores, oedema.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has a poor appetite and has lost weight from his arms and legs. He drinks 80 units a week. His abdomen is distended with shifting dullness. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. A full set of bloods is sent.
questions.q: Which blood result is most likely?
questions.e: Alcohol-related cirrhosis impairs nutrient absorption and metabolism, causing deficiencies of B12, iron and albumin.

steps.x: Cirrhosis + alcohol + poor intake: the liver cannot make **albumin**, and ascites fits.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low albumin.

elim: Not a feature of cirrhosis or malnutrition.
Cirrhosis causes anaemia, including iron and B12 deficiency.
Bilirubin rises in cirrhosis.
Synthetic failure raises the INR.

steps.x: **C. Low albumin.** Alcohol cirrhosis: low B12, iron and albumin.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has 9 months of bloating, cramps and pale, foul-smelling stools. She has lost 5 kg. She now bruises easily and her gums bleed when brushing. Investigations: anti-endomysial antibodies are positive. Her platelet count is 266 × 10⁹/L (150–400) and her PT is 18 seconds (10–14).
questions.q: Which deficiency best explains her bruising?
questions.e: Coeliac disease impairs absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; low vitamin K reduces clotting factors and prolongs the PT.

steps.x: Malabsorption (coeliac) + **prolonged PT** with a normal platelet count = a clotting factor problem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Vitamin K, a fat-soluble vitamin.

elim: Causes macrocytic anaemia, not a prolonged PT.
Causes microcytic anaemia, not bleeding.
Causes macrocytosis and neuropathy.
Scurvy causes bleeding gums but a normal PT.

steps.x: **E. Vitamin K.** Coeliac: deficient A, D, E, K.

questions.stem: A 46 year old homeless man is admitted with 2 months of watery diarrhoea and increasing confusion. He has a rough, darkened rash on the backs of his hands and a broad pigmented band around his neck. He drinks heavily and eats very little. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diarrhoea, dementia and dermatitis with Casal's necklace is pellagra, niacin (B3) deficiency; untreated, the fourth D is death.

clues: darkened rash on the backs of his hands
steps.x: Diarrhoea, dementia, dermatitis = the **4 Ds**. Band around the neck = **Casal's necklace**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pellagra.

elim: Thiamine deficiency: neuropathy or heart failure, not dermatitis.
Protein deficiency in children with oedema.
Vitamin C: perifollicular haemorrhages and bleeding gums.
Confusion with ataxia and ophthalmoplegia, not dermatitis or diarrhoea.

steps.x: **C. Pellagra.** Pellagra = niacin (B3): 4 Ds and Casal's necklace.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with head and neck cancer had eaten almost nothing for 2 weeks. A gastrostomy feed at full target rate was started 2 days ago. Today he has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He has no history of epilepsy and a CT head is normal. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and irregular.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his seizure?
questions.e: A severely malnourished cancer patient fed too fast deteriorates within days with seizures and arrhythmia: refeeding syndrome.

clues: full target rate was started 2 days ago
steps.x: Starved + **feed started fast** + deterioration within days.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Refeeding syndrome.

elim: No alcohol history given, and timing fits the feed.
CT head is normal.
Less likely; the timing after starting a full feed in a starved patient points to refeeding.
He is being fed carbohydrate continuously.

steps.x: **E. Refeeding syndrome.** Deterioration after feeding starts in a starved patient = refeeding syndrome.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 13.8 kg/m². Nasogastric feeding was started 3 days ago. She is now weak, confused and has palpitations. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm. Her ECG shows ectopic beats.
questions.q: Which pattern of blood results is most likely?
o: High phosphate, high potassium, high magnesium
High phosphate, low potassium, low calcium
Low phosphate, high potassium, normal magnesium
Low phosphate, low potassium, low magnesium
Normal phosphate, low sodium, high potassium
questions.e: Refeeding causes an insulin surge driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, with thiamine deficiency too.

clues: Nasogastric feeding was started 3 days ago
steps.x: Refeeding: insulin drives **phosphate, potassium, magnesium** into cells, so all three fall.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: All three low.

elim: The opposite; feeding drives these into cells.
Phosphate falls, not rises, in refeeding.
Potassium also shifts into cells and falls.
Not the refeeding pattern.

steps.x: **D. Low phosphate, low potassium, low magnesium.** Refeeding: low PO4, K and Mg, plus thiamine deficiency.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman is brought to her GP by her mother, who has noticed she eats very little and runs for 2 hours every day. Her periods stopped 8 months ago. She has fine downy hair on her arms. Her BMI is 15.2 kg/m². Her pulse rate is 46 bpm and BP 88/56 mmHg. Thyroid function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her malnutrition?
questions.e: Restricted intake, excessive exercise, amenorrhoea, lanugo and bradycardia with a very low BMI is anorexia nervosa, a recognised cause of malnutrition.

clues: eats very little and runs for 2 hours every day
steps.x: Restriction + over-exercise + amenorrhoea + **lanugo** + bradycardia = eating disorder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anorexia nervosa.

elim: No GI symptoms; the restriction and exercise point elsewhere.
Would give pain, diarrhoea and raised inflammatory markers.
Causes tachycardia; she is bradycardic and thyroid function is normal.
Would give thirst and polyuria.

steps.x: **A. Anorexia nervosa.** Eating disorders are a key cause of malnutrition.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has lost 6 kg over a year. He has loose, pale stools that float and are hard to flush, and abdominal bloating. He has an itchy blistering rash on his elbows and knees. His Hb is 104 g/L with low ferritin and low folate. He eats a normal diet.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his malnutrition?
questions.e: Steatorrhoea, bloating, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency and dermatitis herpetiformis point to coeliac disease causing malabsorption.

clues: itchy blistering rash on his elbows and knees
steps.x: Malabsorption with **dermatitis herpetiformis** and proximal small bowel deficiencies (iron, folate).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coeliac disease.

elim: He eats a normal diet; the problem is absorption.
Steatorrhoea yes, but not the blistering rash or iron and folate deficiency.
Does not cause weight loss, steatorrhoea or deficiencies.
Bloody diarrhoea, not steatorrhoea with a blistering rash.

steps.x: **C. Coeliac disease.** Malabsorption (coeliac) is a key cause of malnutrition.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with alcohol dependence is admitted after eating almost nothing for 3 weeks. He is given IV dextrose and a full diet but no vitamins. Four days later he is breathless with bilateral pitting oedema to the thighs, a raised JVP and warm peripheries. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 104/48 mmHg. Echo shows a dilated, hyperdynamic heart.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Refeeding without thiamine rapidly depletes thiamine, which can precipitate high-output cardiac failure (wet beriberi) or Wernicke's encephalopathy.

clues: IV dextrose and a full diet but no vitamins
steps.x: Carbohydrate given **without thiamine** + **high-output** heart failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wet beriberi.

elim: Gives a poorly contracting heart, not a hyperdynamic one, and does not explain the timing.
Gives oedema but not a raised JVP and high-output state.
Niacin deficiency: diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia.
Thiamine deficiency affecting the brain, not the heart.

steps.x: **E. Wet beriberi.** Thiamine deficiency on refeeding: Wernicke's or wet beriberi.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman is 10 days after a laparotomy for bowel obstruction. She has eaten little for 4 weeks. Her abdominal wound has broken down, and she has developed a urinary tract infection and a sacral pressure sore. Her BMI has fallen from 22 to 18.9 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.4°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying reason for her poor recovery?
questions.e: Catabolism of fat and muscle causes muscle wasting, immune dysfunction and impaired wound healing: wound breakdown, infection and pressure sores after weeks of poor intake.

steps.x: Poor intake + falling BMI + **poor healing**, **infections**, **pressure sore**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Malnutrition.

elim: No history or hyperglycaemia given.
Contributes to fatigue but does not explain the whole picture.
Does not explain the pressure sore, weight loss and UTI.
Causes bone pain and weakness, not poor wound healing.

steps.x: **C. Protein-energy malnutrition.** Malnutrition = poor healing, infections, pressure sores.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has been on an orthopaedic ward for 5 weeks after a complicated hip fracture. He needs help to eat and his meals are often taken away untouched. His weight has fallen by 7 kg. He has no new symptoms, and his inflammatory markers are falling. His BMI is now 18.2 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his weight loss?
questions.e: Long-stay hospital patients who need help eating are a key at-risk group; untouched meals for weeks explain the weight loss.

clues: on an orthopaedic ward for 5 weeks
steps.x: **Long-stay inpatient** + needs help eating + untouched meals.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Malnutrition from poor intake in hospital.

elim: No tremor, tachycardia or heat intolerance.
Possible, but the clear cause is weeks of untouched meals.
Inflammatory markers are falling.
No polyuria or thirst.

steps.x: **A. Hospital-acquired malnutrition from poor intake.** Long-stay hospital patients are at high risk of malnutrition.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is admitted with a fractured wrist. Her usual weight was 60 kg and she now weighs 56 kg (about 7% loss over 4 months). Her BMI is 18.0 kg/m². She has been eating normally until yesterday and is expected to eat again tomorrow. The nurse completes a MUST screen.

visual.title: MUST risk category
visual.label: Her score
visual.caption: A score of 2 or more is high risk.

questions.q: What is her MUST score?
questions.e: MUST: BMI below 18.5 scores 2, 5 to 10% weight loss scores 1, and the acute disease effect (no intake for more than 5 days) is 0, giving 3: high risk.

steps.x: Add the three MUST parts: **BMI** (2), **weight loss** (1), **acute disease** (0).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: 3, high risk (2 or more).

elim: She has both a low BMI and weight loss.
Counts only one of the two.
BMI below 18.5 scores 2, and she also has 5 to 10% weight loss.
The acute disease effect does not apply, as she will eat within 5 days.

steps.x: **D. 3.** MUST = BMI + % weight loss + acute disease effect.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. The ward uses a validated UK tool to screen every new patient for malnutrition risk. His son says he has looked thinner recently. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and oxygen saturation 90% on 2 litres of oxygen.
questions.q: Which set of measures does this screening tool use?
o: BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect
Grip strength, gait speed and falls
Mid-arm circumference, skinfold thickness and BMI
questions.e: MUST assesses BMI, percentage unplanned weight loss and the acute disease effect (likely no nutritional intake for more than 5 days).

steps.x: The validated UK screening tool = **MUST**. Its three steps?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BMI, weight loss, acute disease effect.

elim: Albumin is unreliable and these are not in MUST.
Frailty measures, not MUST.
Anthropometry can help but is not the MUST set.
Not the MUST components.

steps.x: **B. BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect.** MUST: BMI, % weight loss, no intake >5 days.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has lost weight and her GP thinks she may be malnourished. Her BMI is 19.1 kg/m² and her MUST score is 2. Her albumin is 31 g/L (35–50) and CRP 48 mg/L (<5). She asks which test will prove whether she is malnourished.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: There is no single blood test; clinical and nutritional assessment (history, examination, intake, weight trend) is the gold standard. Albumin is distorted by inflammation.

steps.x: No blood test proves malnutrition, and **raised CRP** makes albumin unreliable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical and nutritional assessment.

elim: Measures bone density, not nutritional state.
Albumin also falls with inflammation, as here.
An acute phase reactant, also distorted by inflammation.
Measures one vitamin, not overall nutrition.

steps.x: **A. Clinical and nutritional assessment.** Gold standard = clinical and nutritional assessment.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is in intensive care with pneumonia and septic shock. Before admission he was well, ate normally and had a stable weight with a BMI of 26 kg/m². On day 3 his albumin is 19 g/L (35–50) and his CRP 310 mg/L (<5). A junior doctor wants to start parenteral nutrition because of the albumin.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate interpretation of his albumin?
o: It mainly reflects sepsis, not his nutritional state
questions.e: Albumin is not a reliable nutritional marker on its own: it falls in inflammation, sepsis and liver disease.

clues: stable weight with a BMI of 26 kg/m²
steps.x: Normal BMI, stable weight days ago, now **septic**: albumin is a negative acute phase protein.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sepsis, not malnutrition.

elim: He was well nourished days ago; albumin falls in sepsis.
No proteinuria described, and sepsis explains it.
A very low albumin is expected in septic shock.
No liver history; acute illness explains it.

steps.x: **D. It mainly reflects sepsis, not his nutritional state.** Albumin falls in inflammation, sepsis and liver disease.

questions.stem: An 88 year old woman with mild dementia lives alone and has a carer twice a day. Her MUST score is 1. The community dietitian wants to know exactly what she eats and drinks before advising. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial way to assess her intake?
questions.e: Dietary recall records self-reported food and drink over a set period, often with a carer's food chart.

clues: exactly what she eats and drinks
steps.x: To know **what she eats**, record it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dietary recall or a food diary.

elim: Looks for a swallowing problem, not intake.
A research or ICU tool for energy expenditure.
Not a reliable marker of intake.
Investigates GI pathology, not what she eats.

steps.x: **B. Dietary recall or food diary.** Dietary recall: self-reported intake over a set time.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man is referred by his GP with 6 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months and fatigue. His MUST score is 2. He has no GI symptoms. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. Examination shows muscle wasting only.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate set of initial blood tests?
questions.e: First-line bloods in malnutrition are FBC, U&Es and LFTs, looking for anaemia, electrolyte abnormalities and liver disease.

steps.x: Malnutrition causes **anaemia** and **electrolyte** problems; check the basics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FBC, U&Es, LFTs.

elim: Not a first-line malnutrition test.
No features of infection.
Unreliable on its own.
Not first-line, and they do not assess the effects of malnutrition.

steps.x: **C. FBC, U&Es and LFTs.** Bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFTs.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman admitted with cellulitis has a MUST score of 3. She can swallow safely and eats about half of each meal. She has no GI symptoms and her bowels open normally. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 128/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate nutritional management?
o: Food-first approach with oral nutritional supplements
Observe and repeat MUST in a month
questions.e: A MUST score of 2 or more is high risk: start oral nutritional supplements alongside a food-first approach (fortified, high-calorie, high-protein food). Oral comes before enteral.

clues: eats about half of each meal
steps.x: High risk (**≥2**) but she can eat: stay **oral** and boost it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Food first plus oral supplements.

elim: Oral intake is possible; enteral comes after oral fails.
This is for low risk; a score of 3 is high risk.
Only when the gut cannot be used.
For long-term enteral feeding when oral fails.

steps.x: **A. Food-first approach with oral nutritional supplements.** MUST ≥2: food first + ONS. Oral before enteral before parenteral.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with oesophageal cancer has eaten and drunk almost nothing for 7 days. A nasogastric tube has just been placed and the team is about to start feeding. His BMI is 19.4 kg/m² and his electrolytes are currently normal.
questions.q: Which should be given before the feed is started?
questions.e: With poor or absent intake for more than 5 days, give thiamine before feeding and start slowly, as carbohydrate uses up thiamine.

clues: eaten and drunk almost nothing for 7 days
steps.x: No intake for **more than 5 days** = refeeding risk = **thiamine** first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thiamine.

elim: Not the key vitamin to protect against refeeding.
Not an urgent pre-feeding need.
Extra carbohydrate without thiamine increases risk.
Not related to refeeding.

steps.x: **D. Thiamine.** No intake >5 days: thiamine before feeding.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has had a large left middle cerebral artery stroke. Speech and language therapy assessment shows an unsafe swallow for all food and fluid. His bowel sounds are normal and his abdomen is soft. He is expected to be reassessed in 2 weeks.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate method of feeding?
questions.e: When oral intake is not possible but the gut works, use enteral feeding: an NG tube short term, PEG if longer term.

clues: unsafe swallow for all food and fluid
steps.x: Oral is unsafe, **gut works**, **short term**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: NG tube feeding.

elim: His swallow is unsafe for all oral intake.
Only if the gut cannot be used; his gut works.
For longer-term feeding; his swallow will be reassessed in 2 weeks.
Still oral; the swallow is unsafe for all textures.

steps.x: **A. Nasogastric tube feeding.** Enteral if gut works: NG short term, PEG long term.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman had a small bowel resection 8 days ago. She has a prolonged paralytic ileus with high nasogastric aspirates and absent bowel sounds. She has had no nutrition since surgery. Her BMI is 20.5 kg/m². Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 122/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate nutritional support?
questions.e: When the gut cannot be used, as in prolonged ileus, parenteral nutrition is the next step.

steps.x: Stepwise: oral, enteral, then **parenteral if the gut cannot be used**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Parenteral nutrition.

elim: The gut is not working; feed would just be aspirated.
Still enteral, and she has a generalised ileus.
She cannot absorb oral intake.
Enteral and long-term; the gut cannot be used.

steps.x: **D. Parenteral nutrition.** Gut not usable = TPN.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has lost 7 kg with bloating and pale, foul-smelling stools. Her anti-endomysial antibodies are positive and duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Her Hb is 101 g/L with low ferritin. She is started on iron.
questions.q: Which is the most important long-term management?
questions.e: Long-term management of malnutrition means identifying and treating the cause: for coeliac disease, a strict gluten-free diet.

steps.x: Find and **treat the cause**: coeliac.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gluten-free diet.

elim: Does not treat the cause of malabsorption.
Not first-line for coeliac disease.
For pancreatic insufficiency, not coeliac disease.
Her gut can be used and will recover off gluten.

steps.x: **E. Strict gluten-free diet.** Treat the underlying cause.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman in a care home has a grade 3 sacral pressure sore. She has lost 5 kg over 3 months and her MUST score is 3. The tissue viability nurse has applied an appropriate dressing. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and temperature 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
o: Dietitian review and a pressure-relieving mattress
Strict bed rest on a standard mattress
questions.e: Pressure sores are managed with nutrition and dietitian review, dressings and a supportive mattress.

steps.x: Pressure sore care: **nutrition**, dressings, **mattress**. The dressing is done.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dietitian plus pressure-relieving mattress.

elim: No signs of infection.
Not first-line and she is malnourished.
Increases pressure.
Impairs healing.

steps.x: **A. Dietitian review and a pressure-relieving mattress.** Pressure sores: nutrition, dressings, supportive mattress.

questions.stem: A hospital nutrition team is reviewing five newly admitted patients who are all about to start feeding. Each has a different BMI, recent intake and background. The team wants to decide who needs a slow start with thiamine and daily electrolyte checks.
questions.q: Which patient is at highest risk of refeeding syndrome?
o: BMI 15 with alcohol misuse and 10 days of no intake
BMI 22 after a 2 day fast for surgery
BMI 28 eating normally after an ankle fracture
questions.e: High-risk patients have a low BMI, minimal intake for days, an eating disorder, cancer or cachexia, or alcohol misuse.

steps.x: Look for **low BMI**, **days of little intake**, **alcohol**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The BMI 15 patient with alcohol misuse and no intake.

elim: Normal BMI and a short fast.
Well nourished.
Normal intake.
Well nourished, short illness.

steps.x: **A. BMI 15 with alcohol misuse and 10 days of no intake.** Refeeding risk: low BMI, little intake, eating disorder, cancer, alcohol.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with anorexia nervosa and a BMI of 13.2 kg/m² is starting nasogastric feeding. Feeding will begin at a low rate and thiamine has been given. The consultant asks the junior doctor which blood levels must be checked daily and replaced if low.
questions.q: Which electrolytes should be monitored and replaced?
questions.e: Prevent refeeding: start slowly, give thiamine, and monitor and replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium.

steps.x: The three ions that shift into cells: **phosphate, magnesium, potassium**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Phosphate, magnesium and potassium.

elim: Not the main refeeding electrolytes.
Glucose is watched but phosphate, magnesium and potassium are the key ones.
Renal function is checked, but these are not the key refeeding ions.
Trace elements, not the acute refeeding risk.

steps.x: **B. Phosphate, magnesium and potassium.** Slow feed, thiamine, monitor PO4, Mg and K.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with lung cancer has lost 12 kg over 5 months despite eating some food each day. His arms and thighs have become thin and he struggles to rise from a chair. His BMI is 17.0 kg/m². His HbA1c and thyroid function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the main mechanism of his muscle wasting?
o: Catabolism of muscle protein for energy
questions.e: In malnutrition, fat and muscle stores are broken down for energy, causing progressive muscle wasting, immune dysfunction and poor wound healing.

clues: struggles to rise from a chair
steps.x: Energy deficit: the body **burns its own fat and muscle**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Muscle catabolism.

elim: Myositis, with raised CK and pain.
Motor neurone disease, with fasciculations.
A metabolic myopathy, not cachexia.
Thyroid function is normal.

steps.x: **B. Catabolism of muscle protein for energy.** Malnutrition: catabolism of fat and muscle.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with untreated coeliac disease has aching bones and proximal muscle weakness. Her calcium is 2.08 mmol/L (2.2–2.6), alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L (30–130) and vitamin D low. Her diet contains adequate vitamin D and she spends time outdoors.
questions.q: Which best explains her low vitamin D?
o: Impaired micelle-mediated uptake in damaged small bowel
Increased renal excretion of vitamin D
Liver failure to hydroxylate vitamin D
questions.e: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) need bile salts and micelles for uptake across the small bowel mucosa, which is damaged in coeliac disease.

steps.x: Enough in, enough sun, but **not absorbed**: fat-soluble vitamins need micelles and healthy mucosa.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Impaired micelle uptake across damaged mucosa.

elim: Not the mechanism in coeliac disease.
She spends time outdoors.
No liver disease.
Her diet contains enough.

steps.x: **A. Impaired micelle-mediated uptake in damaged small bowel.** Malabsorption = A, D, E, K deficiency.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 13.9 kg/m² after weeks of minimal intake. Her serum phosphate, potassium and magnesium are all within the normal range on admission. A student concludes she is not at risk of refeeding syndrome.
questions.q: Which best explains why she is still at high risk?
o: Her kidneys will retain too much phosphate
Intracellular stores are depleted despite normal serum levels
Normal levels mean her body has fully adapted
She will develop high potassium when fed
questions.e: Prolonged starvation depletes intracellular phosphate, potassium and magnesium while the body shifts to fat metabolism; serum levels can stay normal until feeding drives them into cells.

clues: all within the normal range on admission
steps.x: Serum levels are a small window; the **cells** are empty.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Depleted intracellular stores.

elim: Phosphate falls on refeeding, it does not accumulate.
Total body stores are low.
Potassium falls on refeeding.
Insulin is low in starvation and surges on feeding.

steps.x: **B. Intracellular stores are depleted despite normal serum levels.** Starvation empties intracellular PO4, K and Mg.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man with alcohol misuse who has eaten little for 2 weeks is given IV glucose for a low blood sugar. Hours later he is confused, unsteady and has nystagmus with bilateral lateral rectus weakness. He had not received any vitamins.
questions.q: Which best explains why the glucose precipitated his symptoms?
o: Niacin is consumed by glucose metabolism
Thiamine is a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism
questions.e: Thiamine (B1) is a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism, so a carbohydrate load uses up scarce thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.

steps.x: Confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia = **Wernicke's**. Glucose uses up **thiamine**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thiamine is needed to metabolise carbohydrate.

elim: Not the mechanism.
Not the cause of Wernicke's.
He was treated for low glucose.
Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, not acute Wernicke's.

steps.x: **E. Thiamine is a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism.** Thiamine before glucose or feeding in at-risk patients.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with alcohol dependence has diarrhoea, memory problems and a scaly, pigmented rash on sun-exposed skin including a band around his neck. He eats very little and lives in a hostel. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. A medical student asks why these particular organs are affected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Impaired DNA synthesis from folate lack
Impaired NAD-dependent energy metabolism in rapidly dividing tissues
Loss of myelin from B12 lack
questions.e: Niacin (B3) is needed to make NAD and NADP; deficiency impairs energy metabolism in rapidly dividing tissues (skin, gut, CNS), giving dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

steps.x: Pellagra (4 Ds). Niacin is the building block of **NAD/NADP**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Impaired NAD/NADP metabolism.

elim: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy).
Causes megaloblastic anaemia.
Causes subacute combined degeneration.
Vitamin A deficiency and night blindness.

steps.x: **C. Impaired NAD-dependent energy metabolism in rapidly dividing tissues.** Niacin = NAD/NADP; skin, gut, brain affected.
